Months in the Making: Appalachian Ski Mountain Prepares for 2026-27 Season

Matt Laws
Nov 17, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:01
Instaread

For skiers and snowboarders, a winter day at Appalachian Ski Mountain might begin by loading up their RFID card or picking up rental equipment. For the people getting the mountain ready, that day has been months in the making.

Appalachian Ski Mountain, along with all of the other resorts, has been hard at work long before the first snow gun fires up for the season. The work stretches across multiple departments – work that goes from refining the online ticket system to finishing building projects.

“We are essentially working all off-season,” Appalachian Ski Mountain’s Director of Marketing Drew Stanley said. “Developing and refining our online ticketing platform, many infrastructure improvements and modifications, recruiting and hiring staff, general facility upgrades and maintenance, etc.”

The Blowing Rock resort’s improvements for the coming season include updates to how and what skiers and snowboarders can purchase online.

“We have continued to develop and refine our 100% custom online ticketing platform, where guests can reserve tickets, rentals, lessons, terrain park passes, memberships, lockers, nursery, and more to make the arrival process feel effortless,” Stanley said. “We offer the only timeslot-based ticketing system in the region. This 5-minute timeslot reservation system has made the check-in process flow better than ever before, ensuring a smooth and fast experience for ticket pickup, rental equipment, and lessons.”

Those refinements will help skiers and boarders get the most out of their time on the snow.

“ASM’s Flex Ticket pairs perfectly with the timeslot reservations, as your ticket time starts when you set foot on the snow, so a guest can arrive at any time on their schedule and get the full value of a day’s ski ticket,” Stanley said.

Outside of the weather, the ticket system has been one of the tougher challenges this off-season.

“Recently, it has been working through and refining our online ticketing platform to ensure the smoothest possible purchase experience for skiers and riders,” Stanley said. “Still a work in progress, but it’s getting there.”

The resort has also continued with construction for both a Snowcat Operations building and a new Skier Services building in addition to opening current Base Lodge square footage to better serve guests. These projects are part of multi-year campaigns.

Terrain park users will also find new features designed for a range of abilities.

“A variety of new terrain park features have been fabricated for the season, with a focus on appealing to all abilities and progression,” Stanley said. “These include wider boxes that are low to the ground and great for learning fundamentals, as well as additional flat boxes that can be set up in a variety of configurations.”

The resort has also added a dedicated RFID entry gate in the Children’s grouping area to make it easy for both the children in the SKIwee and Cruiser Camp Children’s programs to get on the snow, as well as for the parents for drop-off.

Dana Price will also join the team as executive chef, bringing experience in international cuisine to the resort’s dining offerings.

While all those projects bring unique challenges, the biggest task (besides snowmaking, of course) is the personnel puzzle.

“Continuing to hire the right applicants for our team,” Stanley said. “We have many departments, and finding the right people to fit the right positions takes time.”

In addition to finding the right people, Appalachian Ski Mountain has to get them trained so they can be ready to go at a moment’s notice.

“We have several preseason training and orientation sessions depending on department,” Stanley said. “Ultimately, we all need to be flexible on start date, though.”

Guests might be surprised by how many departments have a hand in getting the mountain ready for opening day.

“Probably the amount of departments, coordination, and work from across the board that goes into the operation well before the first skis or snowboards hit the snow,” Stanley said.

As preparations come together, the weather helps determine when the resort can put those months of work into action.

“We are constantly monitoring the weather, and can generally see when a weather window will allow for opening,” Stanley said. “Anything can happen, but modern forecasting has come so far we can usually set our opening day based on a solid forecast 4-5 days out.”

When the snow guns crank on and opening day is near, it brings an incredible atmosphere to the staff.

“It’s an excitement that is hard to describe,” Stanley said. “Something about snow and making snow that brings out a youthful playfulness in anyone who enjoys winter activities.”

About the Author

Matt Laws

Matt is a lifelong resident of the High Country - where he still resides with his wife and son in Roan Mountain, TN. After graduating from East Tennessee State University in 2010 and prior to joining the Appnet family in 2013, he worked for four years as the sports information director at a local Christian college. Matt also has worked for a variety of local newspapers as a sports writer and photographer - something that he still does in the evenings and weekends. In addition to writing and photography, Matt enjoys all types of sports, cooking and traveling.
